notes.written: Written 24 Oct 2026. Figures in the tables update automatically; these summaries are refreshed separately.
themes: The oil shock has flared up again

Brent hit $113 on 22 Oct, its highest close since early May, and WTI is near $99. Houthi drone and missile strikes on Saudi energy sites, Iranian claims of attacks on four tankers in the Gulf and Saudi limits on fuel exports drove the jump.
Inflation is still rising in most places

September inflation: UK 3.5% (3.4% expected), Canada 3.1%, US 3.7%, euro area 3.8%, Japan core 2.1% (first time above 2% in nine months) and Switzerland 1.0%, a two-year high. New Zealand was the exception, easing to 3.7% as petrol fell during the quarter.
Decision week: mostly holds now, rises later

The RBNZ, Bank of Canada and Fed decide on 28 Oct, the ECB on 29 Oct and the BoJ on 30 Oct. Most are expected to hold this time, but a Reuters poll found all 100 economists expect a Fed rise in December. An RBNZ rise is widely expected, and Canada is a close call.
Next up: Australia and the UK
The RBA decides on 3 Nov, with markets split close to 50/50 on a rise. The Bank of England decides on 5 Nov, and markets put the chance of a rise to 4% above 90% after the inflation jump.

UK consumer confidence fell to −24 from −13 and retail sales dropped 0.4% in September. Euro-area services surveys slipped to 51.7 and investor mood (ZEW) to 18.5. Higher fuel bills and borrowing costs are the common complaint.

Higher oil means more inflation worry and more expected rate rises, which keeps real yields high (the US 10-year near 5%, about 2.6% after inflation). Gold briefly fell below $4,000 on 23 Oct, its lowest since early August, and is down about 15% in six months; silver is down about 30%.

USD.note: Raised on 16 Sep to 3.75–4.00%, the first rise since 2023. Expected to hold on 28 Oct; economists widely expect another rise in December.

EUR.note: Raised in June and on 10 Sep (deposit rate 2.50%) and says inflation will stay above target for some time. Expected to hold on 29 Oct and judge a further rise in December, with new forecasts.

GBP.note: Held at 3.75% on 17 Sep, but 3 of 9 members voted to raise to 4%. After September inflation came in at 3.5%, markets see a rise on 5 Nov as very likely.

JPY.note: Raised on 18 Sep to the highest since 1995. Governor Ueda says rates will keep rising, but markets expect a hold on 30 Oct and see December as more likely for the next move.

CAD.note: On hold at 2.25% at every meeting this year. Underlying inflation is below 2%, but high oil prices make the 28 Oct decision a close call.

AUD.note: Raised to 4.60% on 29 Sep, unanimously, and said it could go further. Markets see the 3 Nov decision as close to a coin flip.

NZD.note: Raised twice (to 2.75% on 2 Sep) but signalled a more measured pace. A rise to 3.00% on 28 Oct is widely expected, though softer Q3 inflation gives it room to wait.

CHF.note: Held at 0% on 24 Sep and stands ready to sell francs if needed. Inflation has crept up to the 1% mid-point of its 0–2% range.

CNY.note: Lending rates unchanged again on 20 Oct (1-year 3.00%); growth support comes mostly from the government.

stories.USD: Inflation is running at 3.7% and producer prices jumped in September, so the Fed, which raised rates to 3.75–4.00% in September, is expected to raise again in December (all 100 economists in a Reuters poll agree), though probably not on 28 October. Hiring has slowed sharply (only 29,000 jobs in September, unemployment 4.2%) and housing starts fell 5.2%, yet shoppers keep spending (retail sales +0.8%) and sentiment edged up to 48.0. The 10-year yield is near 5%, about 2.6% after inflation. Next: Fed 28 Oct, Q3 GDP (3.2% expected) and the Fed’s preferred inflation measure (core PCE) 29 Oct, wage costs 30 Oct, October jobs report 6 Nov.
stories.EUR: Euro-area inflation is 3.8%, the highest in three years, but only 2.5% without food and energy, so the energy shock has not yet spread widely. The ECB has raised its deposit rate twice to 2.50%. The mood is souring: October business surveys slipped (services 51.7 from 53.0, factories 52.4), investor mood (ZEW) fell to 18.5 from 25.8 and consumer confidence dropped to −18. The trade balance has swung into deficit (−€6.8bn) as energy imports cost more. Unemployment is steady at 6.4%. Next: ECB 29 Oct (a hold is expected), German inflation, euro-area Q3 GDP and unemployment 30 Oct.
stories.GBP: Inflation jumped to 3.5% in September, above the 3.4% expected, as petrol and diesel prices rose almost 30% on a year. Core inflation is 2.8% and services 3.7%. The Bank of England held at 3.75% in September with three members voting for 4%, and markets now see a rise on 5 November as very likely. Activity is mixed: business surveys jumped (services 53.1) and unemployment fell to 4.7%, but pay growth is cooling (3.7%), retail sales fell 0.4% and consumer confidence slumped to −24, a six-month low, on fuel bills and tax worries. Next: Autumn Budget 28 Oct, Bank of England 5 Nov.
stories.JPY: The Bank of Japan raised rates to 1.25% on 18 September, the highest since 1995, and Governor Ueda says more rises are coming, but markets expect it to wait until after 30 October. National core inflation rose to 2.1% in September, above the 2% target for the first time in nine months, and Tokyo’s early reading is 2.7%. Households are still cutting back (spending −3.1% on a year) and dearer energy has pushed the trade balance to a deficit (−¥0.70tn). The interest-rate gap still favours the dollar (USD/JPY around 158). Next: Tokyo inflation and jobs 29 Oct (UK evening), BoJ with new forecasts 30 Oct.
stories.CAD: Headline inflation rose to 3.1% in September, driven by petrol (+27.8% on a year), but underlying measures eased (median 1.9%, trimmed 1.8%) and grocery inflation slowed to 1.7%. The Bank of Canada has held at 2.25% all year, and the 28 October decision is seen as a close call: oil keeps inflation high while jobs are disappearing (68,300 lost in September, unemployment 6.5%). Shoppers held up in August (retail sales +1.2%), and high oil prices help Canada’s exports (trade surplus C$4.2bn). Next: Bank of Canada with new forecasts 28 Oct, GDP 30 Oct, federal budget 5 Nov.
stories.AUD: The RBA raised rates to 4.60% on 29 September and said it could go further, with inflation at 4.0% and households expecting 5.3%. Markets now see the 3 November decision as close to a coin flip, so this week’s inflation figure matters a lot. The economy is softening: 39,300 jobs lost in September, unemployment up to 4.7%, household spending flat and business confidence negative (NAB −13). China, Australia’s biggest customer, grew a little faster in Q3 (4.5%), which helps. Next: September CPI 28 Oct (4.2% expected), RBA 3 Nov.
stories.NZD: Inflation eased to 3.7% in the year to September, from 4.1%, below the 3.8% expected and the RBNZ’s own 3.9% forecast, because petrol fell 6.5% during the quarter. It is still above the 1–3% target band, core inflation is 2.9% and price rises are spreading across more items. The RBNZ has raised rates twice to 2.75%, and a rise to 3.00% on 28 October was widely expected before the data; the softer figure gives it room to wait. The economy is weak (GDP +0.2% in Q2, unemployment 5.6%, trade deficit NZ$1.97bn in September). Next: RBNZ 28 Oct (UK 01:00), ANZ business confidence 29 Oct.
stories.CHF: Switzerland is the outlier: inflation is only 1.0% (September, a two-year high on heating oil and fuel), and the SNB holds at 0% and stands ready to sell francs if needed. The franc is a safe haven that tends to gain when global worries rise. The economy is strong: GDP jumped 1.5% in Q2 (1.9% including big sporting events), factories are still expanding (PMI 55.3), shoppers are spending (retail +3.2% on a year) and unemployment is low at 3.1%. Next: no big Swiss releases on the calendar in the coming week; the next SNB decision is in December.
stories.CNY: China is shown because it drives AUD, NZD and commodity demand. Growth picked up to 4.5% on a year in Q3, from 4.3%, beating forecasts and meeting the 4.5–5% target, thanks mostly to exports (trade surplus $133.5bn in September). Factory output rose 5.5%, but home demand is weak: retail sales grew only 1.1% and investment is down 7.2% so far this year as the property slump continues. Inflation is low (0.9%) and lending rates were left at 3.00%. Next: official factory and services surveys 31 Oct.

oil.title: Oil (WTI and Brent)
oil.what: The price of crude oil. Brent is the global benchmark, WTI the US one.
oil.now: Brent is up about 11% in six months and WTI about 7%, and Brent hit $113 on 22 Oct, its highest close since early May. The Middle East conflict is the driver: Houthi strikes on Saudi energy sites, Iranian claims of attacks on tankers in the Gulf and Saudi limits on fuel exports. Any easing, or more output from OPEC+, would pull prices back.
oil.links: High oil helps oil exporters (CAD) and hurts importers (JPY, EUR). It feeds straight into inflation, which is why central banks have turned to raising rates.

gold.title: Gold
gold.what: Gold priced in US dollars. It pays no interest, so it competes with what investors can earn elsewhere.
gold.now: Down about 15% in six months, and briefly below $4,000 on 23 Oct, its lowest since early August. Higher oil feeds inflation worries and bets on more Fed rate rises, which keeps real interest rates high (US 10-year after inflation near 2.6%). Central banks buying record amounts (288.9 tonnes in Q2) and safe-haven demand during the conflict are the support.
gold.links: Gold tends to rise when real yields fall, the dollar weakens or fear spikes. It often moves with CHF and JPY as a safe haven, and with AUD, since Australia is a big producer.

silver.title: Silver
silver.what: Half precious metal, half industrial metal (solar panels, electronics), so it swings more than gold.
silver.now: Down about 30% in six months, roughly double gold’s fall, with another drop of about 3.6% on 23 Oct: the same rate headwind, plus worries about factory demand as growth slows.
silver.links: Follows gold in direction but with bigger swings; weaker Chinese industry weighs on it.
